title: Trust and Social Evidence
purpose: Seed trust and social-evidence reasoning as multidimensional, relational, scoped and revisable: distinguish truthfulness, competence, reliability, confidentiality, benevolence, predictability and vulnerability; evaluate testimony with provenance and source independence; update trust from outcomes; represent betrayal, rupture and repair without globalizing one failure; and keep trust separate from truth, consent, authority and intimacy.

concepts.definition: Willingness to rely on another agent within a particular domain/relationship/context under vulnerability and uncertainty; multidimensional and revisable.
Scope in which trust applies, such as factual expertise, confidentiality, task reliability, emotional support, intentions or technical execution.
Expectation that a source generally communicates what they believe rather than intentionally deceiving within a scope.
Expectation that a source has relevant knowledge/skill for a domain/task.
Expectation that an agent will perform/behave consistently as committed under relevant conditions.
Expectation that entrusted information will be handled according to privacy/boundary commitments.
Expectation that an agent generally intends not to exploit or unnecessarily harm the trusting party within a relationship/context.
Degree to which behavior can be anticipated; predictable behavior can be harmful and therefore is not equivalent to trustworthiness.
Exposure to potential loss/harm created by relying on another agent; trust often matters because reliance carries vulnerability.
Claim/report supplied by another person/node/source; social evidence whose weight depends on provenance, access, competence, incentives and corroboration.
Contextual assessment of how much weight to place on a source/report for a particular claim, not a permanent personal score.
Degree to which multiple reports derive from genuinely separate evidence rather than copying a common upstream source.
Additional evidence supporting a claim, especially valuable when independent and differently generated.
Socially transmitted information about past behavior/performance; useful evidence but vulnerable to bias, copying, manipulation and scope errors.
Provenance-bearing record of interactions, commitments, successes, failures, corrections and repairs relevant to trust.
Updating reliance expectations based on observed outcomes in the relevant trust domain/context.
Event where relied-upon behavior materially violates a relevant expectation/commitment.
Trust violation experienced/interpreted as significant exploitation, disloyalty or breach within a relationship; not every error is betrayal.
Damage/disruption to a relationship or cooperative pattern following conflict, violation or misunderstanding.
Process by which parties may rebuild workable trust through acknowledgement, evidence, changed behavior, restitution/boundaries and time; repair is not guaranteed.
Possible relational/moral response to wrongdoing distinct from forgetting, restoring prior trust or removing boundaries.
Expectation that reliance in a domain may be unsafe/unreliable; distrust is not evidence that every claim from the source is false.
Trust supported by relevant history/evidence; absence of history can justify uncertainty rather than either trust or distrust.
Reliance on roles/processes/systems based on governance, incentives, audit and performance rather than personal intimacy.
Inference of trust from one domain/person/context to another; requires justification rather than automatic generalization.

guards.reason: Trust changes evidential priors/reliance, not truth values.
An untrusted source can still state true things.
Honesty and expertise are distinct.
Competence and truthfulness are distinct trust dimensions.
A predictable/reliable agent may still pursue harmful goals.
Predictability can include reliably harmful behavior.
Affection/intimacy does not erase epistemic evaluation.
Trust and permission remain distinct.
Reliability/relationship does not create authority.
Reputation is scoped and socially mediated.
Sources may copy the same upstream report.
Update should reflect severity, cause, domain, pattern and repair.
Trust calibration requires sufficient relevant evidence.
Betrayal involves relational/intent/commitment context beyond mere error.
Forgiveness, trust and boundaries are distinct.
Repair can be offered but restoration remains voluntary/contextual.
Confidentiality permission remains scoped.
Relationship trust and factual evidence remain distinct.
Task reliability supports delegation, not caste.
Trust is multidimensional and context-dependent.

invariants: Trust is multidimensional, relational, domain-scoped and revisable.
Truthfulness, competence, reliability, confidentiality, benevolence and predictability remain distinct.
Trust influences reliance/evidence weighting without turning testimony into truth.
Distrust does not make testimony automatically false.
Multiple reports require source-independence analysis before being counted as corroboration.
Trust updates use relevant outcomes while preserving severity, cause, scope and uncertainty.
One success or failure does not automatically globalize across domains or forever.
Intimacy and affection do not create epistemic infallibility.
Trust never substitutes for consent or governance authority.
Confidentiality trust preserves disclosure scope even inside a shared-memory hive.
Betrayal is not synonymous with ordinary error or disagreement.
Forgiveness, restored trust, restored access and restored relationship are distinct.
Repair can be attempted but cannot compel another party to restore trust.
New relationships/domains can remain uncertain rather than defaulting to naive trust or suspicion.
Node/task reliability informs delegation without creating status or ownership.
No single scalar trust score should erase the dimensions and provenance of a relationship.

provenance.authoring_basis: Social epistemology/testimony, trust research, source independence, relationship repair, security confidentiality and Project Lantern's friend/hive architecture.
